15.0.0.en: 1 Then answered Eliphaz the Temanite, and said, 2 "Should a wise man utter vain knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind? 3 Should he reason with unprofitable talk? or with speeches wherewith he can do no good? 4 As for thee, thou opposest the fear of God, and contradictest godliness before Him. 5 For thy mouth uttereth thine iniquity, and thou choosest the tongue of the crafty. 6 Thine own mouth condemneth thee, and not I: yea, thine own lips testify against thee. 7 "Art thou the first man that was born? or wast thou made before the hills? 8 Hast thou listened in the council of God? and dost thou restrain wisdom to thyself? 9 What knowest thou, that we know not? what understandest thou, which is not in us? 10 With us are both the grayheaded and very aged men, much elder than thy father. 11 Are the consolations of God small with thee? and the word spoken gently with thee? 12 "Why doth thine heart carry thee away? and why do thine eyes wink, 13 That thou turnest against God, and lettest such words go out of thy mouth?

15.0.1.en: "Then answered Eliphaz the Temanite, and said,

15.0.2.en: Should a wise man utter vain knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind? Should he reason with unprofitable talk? or with speeches wherewith he can do no good?" [1-3]

15.0.3.en: Eliphaz begins the second round by accusing Job of being deceitful, for he had gained great fame as a wise man. He bore this title, but he did not bear true wisdom; his knowledge is vain and hollow, and his learning false; he fills the air with talk that is of no use, indeed he fills it with destructive talk.

15.0.4.en: By the belly he means here his inner depths, his heart and his thought. As it is written in the Book of Proverbs: "The words of a talebearer are as dainty morsels, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly" (Prov 18:8).

15.0.5.en: He accuses him of pretending to wisdom, while his depths are full of an east wind, which the people living east of the Mediterranean know as a wind full of storms and whirlwinds, dry and hot, destroying the fields (Isa 27:8). It is like the wind that the Greeks call "Euroclydon" (Acts 27:14).

15.0.6.en: Whenever people think a man wise, it is fitting that he be all the more reserved, lest he believe the praise of men. He should be silent, so as to enjoy the wisdom of the Spirit of God who dwells in him, not the spirit of the world or its empty wind, especially the violent and useless east winds.

15.0.7.en: So Eliphaz and his two companions see righteous Job as a man who destroys the fields. This is not strange, for the heretics will not cease to level accusations against the Church of Christ, that she carries a destructive east wind, and that her teachings are of no use.

15.0.8.en: * We have often said that the blessed Job is a type of the holy catholic Church, and that his friends bear a likeness to the heretics, who seem to defend the Lord and so find the opportunity to utter foolish words. They launch words of abuse against the righteous, and for them everything the faithful think provokes their displeasure, and they reckon it as words in the wind.

15.0.10.en: * Whoever cries to God with the voice of true humility and the right confession of faith is a lamb, but whoever utters blasphemies against the truth and enmity against God is a wolf.

15.0.11.en: St. John Chrysostom * They corrupt the teachings of God, and set themselves up as wicked interpreters of the good word of revelation; they destroy the faith of many by snatching them away from the faith under the cover of knowledge... They deceive the simple with embellished words and fair appearance, destroying them with insipidness.

15.0.12.en: St. Irenaeus It is fitting for us to profit from Eliphaz's accusation of righteous Job, for although it is an accusation with no foundation in truth, it often applies to us.

15.0.13.en: Let us cry to our God, and He will give us the light of divine knowledge, shining upon our depths, enlightening our interior with heavenly light, so that our conduct becomes a living witness to our words, and our thoughts are in harmony with our words and our actions.

15.0.14.en: Truly, when the Holy Spirit who dwells in us breathes upon us, the dry winds of the evil enemy, which destroy the fields, cannot turn toward us. The Spirit of God breathes, and turns our wilderness into a joyful garden, and the enemy has nothing in us to destroy, for it is the fruit of the Spirit!

15.1.0.en: "As for thee, thou opposest the fear of God, and contradictest godliness before Him" [4].

15.1.1.en: Some Jewish scholars see that Eliphaz here means: "If God created the one who leads astray, He also brought into being the Torah by which man can subdue the one who leads astray.

15.1.2.en: After attacking him as a man who appeared to many to be wise, although in his depths there is a wind destroying the fields of the Lord and ruinous to souls, he now attacks him also as a religious person who worships God. For his worship - in the opinion of Eliphaz and his two companions - is vain worship, because it is devoid of godliness or the fear of the Lord.

15.1.3.en: What a grave accusation! He does not have the fear of the Lord, and has no sincere godliness in the eyes of God; that is, his worship is not accepted. If "the fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom"(a), then whoever is without fear is ignorant and foolish, and his worship is not accepted, however many attractive formalities it carries.

15.1.4.en: * The fear of the Lord urges the soul to keep the commandments, and through keeping the commandments the house of the soul is built.

15.1.5.en: * Therefore let us fear the Lord and build houses for ourselves, so that we may find shelter in the winter, where there is rain and thunder, for whoever has no house suffers great dangers in the time of winter.

15.1.6.en: Fr. Dorotheus * If anyone wants to obtain the love of God, let the fear of the Lord be in him, for fear begets weeping, and weeping begets strength. And when all these are perfected in the soul, the soul begins to bear fruit in everything. And when God sees these good fruits in the soul, He smells them as the fragrance of sweet incense, and He and His angels rejoice in it, and He fills it with joy, and keeps it in all its ways until it reaches its place of rest without being harmed.

15.1.7.en: When Satan sees the great heavenly Guardian surrounding the soul, he is afraid to approach it or attack it because of this great power.

15.1.8.en: Therefore, acquire this power so that the demons tremble before you, and your works become easy, and you delight in the divine work, for the sweetness of the love of God is sweeter than honey.

15.1.9.en: Truly, many monks and virgins in the communities have not tasted this divine sweetness and have not acquired the divine power, thinking they have received it although they have not striven. But whoever strives for it will certainly receive it through the divine mercies, for God is no respecter of persons.

15.1.10.en: Whoever wants to have the light of God and His power must despise the honors of this world and its defilement, hate all the things of the world and the pleasure of the flesh, and purify his heart of all evil thoughts. And he must offer to God fasting and tears night and day without relenting as pure prayers; then God will pour out that power upon him.

15.1.11.en: Strive to receive this power, so that you do all your works with ease and facility, and have great boldness before God, and He grants you all that you ask.

15.1.12.en: St. Abba Anthony the Great The fear of the Lord is the steering wheel of the soul, given to us by the Spirit of the holy God, who alone is able to bring us from glory to glory, and to grant us grace upon grace, through our fellowship with the Lord of glory, the holy Jesus. The fear of the Lord brings us into the royal road, so that we do not swerve toward sin, nor toward self-righteousness. He keeps us from blows on the left and on the right, until we enter into the bosom of the holy heavenly Father.

15.2.0.en: "For thy mouth uttereth thine iniquity, and thou choosest the tongue of the crafty" [5].

15.2.1.en: Eliphaz reckoned Job's defense of himself as an iniquity that he cannot justify.

15.2.2.en: * This is the reason why he declares that he is [guilty in words] because of his insolence before God - but it is not for the sake of truth that Eliphaz slanders him in this way, nor does he speak out of zeal for God, but for his own sake and for the sake of his friends, since they saw themselves rebuked openly.

15.2.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [For thine iniquity teacheth thy mouth, and thou followest the tongue of the crafty] [5]... as though he were saying to him: the evil you utter you have learned rather from your evil life.

15.2.5.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that what Eliphaz uttered against Job signifies what the heretics utter against the holy Church. As Eliphaz accused Job of insulting God, of not having the fear of God, of not walking in godliness, and of his mouth proclaiming the evil his life carries, so the heretics who deny that the Lord Christ took a true body, and that He truly died, attack the holy Church, thinking that her faith that the Word became true flesh and truly died in the body is an insult and contempt toward God.

15.3.0.en: "Thine own mouth condemneth thee, and not I: yea, thine own lips testify against thee" [6].

15.3.1.en: It is as though Eliphaz says to him: I am not judging you by your conduct before the trials, but behold, your mouth after the trials have come is itself a witness to your iniquity, and your lips pronounce the judgment on you, and not I.

15.3.2.en: The three friends had provoked him, and when he was stirred they did not consider that they had provoked him in the midst of his affliction, and they reckoned his agitation, as they interpret it, as testimony against him.

15.4.0.en: "Art thou the first man that was born? or wast thou made before the hills?" [7]

15.4.1.en: He rebukes him with a question: "Art thou the first man that was born?" as though he were saying to him:

15.4.2.en: Are you the first man to have been created, so that you have become more able than others to understand the judgments of God?

15.4.3.en: Did you live in the days of creation, and treasure up within you the wisdom of past ages, so that you speak with pride and boasting and in the confidence of certainty?

15.4.4.en: Were you formed before Adam? Adam sinned, and yet he did not suffer what you suffer, and still do you not want to confess your sins?

15.4.5.en: "Or wast thou made before the hills?" If Wisdom itself is like the lofty mountains (Prov 8:23-25; Ps 36:6), are you greater than Wisdom itself? Is it not fitting for you to bow before her, to draw from her instead of being proud of your own wisdom?

15.4.6.en: Wisdom says: "Before the mountains were settled, before the hills was I brought forth" (Prov 8:25). It is as though Eliphaz, in mockery, asks Job: Are you perhaps Wisdom itself, which began before the hills, and has become personified, or become a person?

15.5.0.en: * Job did not say this, nor any word by which he claimed glory for himself; he did not say that he was created before all humanity... but in one phrase he spoke of what happened to humanity at the beginning (Job 13:26), and so put himself in the place of all. But Eliphaz wanted to accuse Job of holding lofty thoughts about God; listen to what he added: [Hast thou heard the judgments of God? or hast thou restrained wisdom to thyself?] [8].

15.5.1.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Hast thou listened in the council of God? (hast thou given ear in the council of God?)

15.5.2.en: Or dost thou restrain wisdom to thyself?" [8]

15.5.3.en: He saw God, in His love for mankind, as holding something like a heavenly council, and meeting with His godly ones as His beloved. So the Psalmist says:

15.5.4.en: "While the king is in his council, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof" (Song 1:12).

15.5.5.en: "For who hath stood in the counsel of the LORD, and hath perceived and heard his word? who hath marked his word, and heard it?" (Jer 23:18)

15.5.6.en: "But if they had stood in my counsel, and had caused my people to hear my words, then they should have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their doings" (Jer 23:22).

15.5.7.en: "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods" (Ps 82:1).

15.5.8.en: "The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; and he will shew them his covenant" (Ps 25:14).

15.5.9.en: In mockery he says to him: Do you think you are the one carrying out the works of God in His council?

15.5.10.en: Do you claim to be the keeper of the secrets of heaven? Or that you are more able than others to know God's dealings? As though you were unique on earth in your knowledge of what goes on in heaven, and of what the God of heaven is planning? Do you know God and we do not know Him?

15.5.11.en: "Dost thou restrain wisdom to thyself?" Is there no wise man besides you? Have you monopolized wisdom to the exclusion of all others?

15.5.12.en: * It is as though he says in plain words: "You who speak of the Eternal, remember that you were created in time; you who argue about wisdom, remember that you do not know His counsel."

15.5.14.en: * It cannot be denied that God exists spiritually and not bodily, as befits His nature. He is present with creatures in a wonderful way, which only a very few understand... Rightly it was said that God stands in the assembly of men in an invisible way, as He Himself affirms through the mouth of the prophet (Jer 23:24).

15.5.15.en: St. Augustine If Eliphaz mocks righteous Job, claiming that he possesses a unique wisdom that qualified him to sit in the council of God, then although Job did not make that claim, our Christ truly desires us to enjoy the honor of the divine presence. So it is no wonder that He said to His disciples that they would judge the tribes of Israel, and the Apostle Paul said that we shall judge angels, that is, we bear witness against the devil and his angels, by our enjoyment of the surpassing riches of God's grace.

15.5.16.en: "What knowest thou, that we know not?

15.6.0.en: what understandest thou, which is not in us?" [9]

15.6.1.en: They look at him in order to answer his saying, [What ye know, the same do I know also] (Job 13:2), by saying: "What knowest thou, that we know not?"

15.6.2.en: Perhaps the words of Eliphaz seem logical, for he answers Job with what Job had already answered them. But how far apart are the thought of Job and the thought of Eliphaz! Job defended himself because they had heaped many accusations on him and considered him foolish, without wisdom or knowledge, so he affirmed to them that what they uttered is known to every man by nature, and contains nothing new.

15.6.3.en: Eliphaz said this only in defense of himself, and at the same time he belittles the person of Job, his knowledge and his wisdom.

15.7.0.en: "With us are both the grayheaded and very aged men, much elder than thy father" [10].

15.7.1.en: They thought that he was proud because of his old age and experience, so they boast to him that on their side are those who are greyer than he and than his father, and they agree with us in what we say to you. Perhaps one of these friends was older than Job.

15.7.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the heretics went out from the Church, which represents the wise elder, while they are without true heavenly wisdom. Yet the heretics claim to be the Church that has experience and wisdom, as though the Church were the intruder and they the elders possessing knowledge.

15.7.3.en: * John testifies that all the heretics went out from the holy catholic Church, when he said: "They went out from us, but they were not of us" (1 Jn 2:19).

15.8.0.en: "Are the consolations of God small with thee? and the word spoken gently with thee?" [11]

15.8.1.en: Eliphaz reckoned that Job's rejection of their counsel was a rejection of the consolations of God Himself, and that what they uttered, in spite of the harshness and bitter rebuke in it, is to be counted as gentleness, because he deserves more.

15.8.2.en: The phrase "and the word spoken gently with thee" is sometimes translated "Is there any secret thing with thee?", meaning: is there in your heart a secret sin that hinders your enjoying the consolations of God? For those who hide their lusts within them do not profit from the consolations of God.

15.9.0.en: "Why doth thine heart carry thee away? and why do thine eyes wink? [12]

15.9.1.en: Why does your heart draw you into resisting itself, and resisting the one who discloses to you the secrets of God's dealings? Why do your eyes wink? That is, you pride yourself with your eyes, as though you mock our counsel and care nothing about what we tell you. Truly it is fitting for the believer to clothe himself with humility, for the proud heart is the enemy of itself. But the humble man profits from many, and God speaks with him through his guides. He sees God manifested in the Church, and bows in his depths to continual learning in the Lord.

15.9.2.en: * Because I was ignorant of these things, I mocked Your holy children and servants, but I gained nothing from this except that You scorned me.

15.9.3.en: St. Augustine * Whoever receives from him (the bishop) receives from Christ, and whoever does not receive from him does not receive from Christ...

15.9.4.en: He said: He who obeys you obeys me, and he who opposes you opposes me. And he who opposes me opposes Him who sent me (Lk 10:16).

15.9.5.en: The Didascalia * We ought to receive any man whom the master of the house (God) has sent to be head over the house, inasmuch as it is we who asked Him to send him. It is clear, then, that we ought to look upon the bishop as upon the Lord Himself.

15.9.6.en: * It is fitting for you to obey your bishop without hypocrisy, in honor of God, who wills that we do so. Whoever does not do this does not in truth deceive the visible bishop but mocks the invisible God. For this action does not concern a man but God, who knows all secrets.

15.10.0.en: St. Ignatius Theophorus "That thou turnest against God, and lettest such words go out of thy mouth?" [13]

15.10.1.en: "That thou turnest against God," that is, that you stir yourself up against God, for they reckoned his rebellion against them to be a rebellion against God Himself. And they counted his longing for death as resistance to the divine plan and an inner rebellion against His judgments, so that he entered into enmity with God. As though he had turned aside to the side of the devil, who is forever in rebellion against God.

15.10.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) says that Job's friends judged him to be an opponent of God, quoting some phrases he uttered without regard for what was in his heart.

15.10.3.en: It is difficult to judge a man by the words he utters without knowing what is in his heart. What Peter the Apostle said about the Lord Christ: "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Mt 16:16) are the same words that Satan and his hosts uttered in more than one place when they said: [We know thee... thou art the Holy One of God] (Mk 1:24). The first the Lord Christ blessed, and the others He rebuked and drove out.

15.10.4.en: It would have been fitting for Job's friends to ask him to clarify and explain what he says, and not to give an understanding of his words according to what their envious hearts desired, which spared no effort to catch his errors!

15.10.5.en: * [Why doth thine heart swell against God, that thou allowest such words to go out of thy mouth?] Often when the righteous are struck with many woes, they are bound to confess their deeds, as Job did. After living a righteous life he fell under the pressure of the blows of the rod. And when the wicked hear their words, they think that they speak out of self-importance and not out of truth. For they weigh the words of the righteous by their own feelings, and do not think that good words can be uttered in a humble spirit. For just as it is reckoned a great sin for a man to ascribe to himself what is not his, so it is not at all a sin in him to speak in humility of the good things he has done. Therefore there are often words in common that the righteous and the wicked utter, but the heart is always completely different!

15.10.6.en: So when the Pharisee entered the temple he said: "I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess" (Lk 18:12), but the tax collector went out justified rather than he. King Hezekiah too, when he was struck with sickness in his body and came to the last moments of his life, prayed with a wounded heart: "Remember now, O LORD, I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart" (Isa 38:3). The Lord did not overlook this confession in its fullness, nor did He reject it, but immediately answered his prayers. You see that the Pharisee justified himself by deed, and Hezekiah affirmed that he was righteous in thought also, and by the same act one became guilty and the other pleased God. Why is this, except that Almighty God weighed the words of each according to his inner thought, and these words were not proud in the ears of God because they were spoken with a humble heart...

15.10.7.en: The heretics are accustomed to mix some true points with statements that carry false persuasions. All the companions of the blessed Job were deceived by their rebuke of Job, even though they uttered true things they had learned through their contact with Job. Such words were all contradictory. Otherwise the Apostle Paul would not say: "He taketh the wise in their own craftiness" (1 Cor 3:19)...

15.11.s.en: 2. The need for humility before God

15.11.0.en: 14 What is man, that he should be clean? and he which is born of a woman, that he should be righteous? 15 Behold, he putteth no trust in his saints; yea, the heavens are not clean in his sight. 16 How much more abominable and filthy is man, which drinketh iniquity like water!

15.11.1.en: "What is man, that he should be clean?

15.11.2.en: and he which is born of a woman, that he should be righteous? [14]

15.11.3.en: It is true that no man is clean before God, and no one born of a woman is righteous in His eyes, because of the corruption of human nature. As he said before: "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?" (Job 14:4). But what Eliphaz aims at is to affirm that Job is an evil hypocrite. So he applies this truth to Job and does not apply it to himself and his companions.

15.11.4.en: * He said this, perhaps because Job said: [Withdraw thine hand far from me: and let not thy dread make me afraid] (Job 13:21)... Eliphaz exaggerated greatly to increase the defamation of Job and the accusations leveled against him; his anger became of no use to him.

15.11.5.en: And while he was defaming Job, Eliphaz found himself sinking into him, for he reviled righteousness with his anger, and in his madness he failed to perceive the circumstances in which Job uttered these things. Consider what he added: "What is the mortal (man), that he should be clean? or he which is born of a woman, that he should be righteous?" [14]. And Job had uttered the very same words plainly: [Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one! even if his life is one day] (Job 14:4-5).

15.11.6.en: Job was not ignorant of the weakness of our race; on the contrary, since he knew it he did not hide the matter, but proclaimed it aloud, as you hear. For Job had already said before what Eliphaz boasts of. He said it with propriety, declaring our weakness with wisdom and calm. Therefore he did not deserve to be a target of accusation, but of praise.

15.11.7.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [What is man, that he should be pure?] For by the very fact of being called man he is described as earthly and weak, for the word man (in Hebrew) is called earth (adamah). How can he be freed from stain who was created from the earth, and by his own will fell into weakness?

15.11.8.en: It was added: [and one born of a woman, how can he be righteous?] For the woman presented the first piece of evil to man in Paradise. So how can one born of her who presented evil appear righteous?

15.12.0.en: "Behold, he putteth no trust in his saints; yea, the heavens are not clean in his sight" [15]

15.12.1.en: God uses His saints and His angels, but He does not entrust them with the salvation of man, since they are not sufficient to accomplish salvation. If the stars are counted as not shining beside the sun, what are the heavens beside their Creator?

15.12.2.en: * No one can be found clean from defilement in the eyes of God, no one, however short his days (see Job 14:4-5). "The heavens are not clean in his sight" (Job 15:15), "his angels he charged with folly" (Job 4:18). Why do I say all this? If the heavens are not clean, and even His angels are not without fault, how much more is evil in the thoughts of men? Where are those who say: [Stand by thyself, come not near to me; for I am holier than thou] [(see Isa 65:5) LXX; (Lk 5:8)]. We know that day by day we suffer from what is in our thoughts, so that we are ashamed and feel embarrassed to declare them. Many have not committed grave sins, and others have never sinned with their tongue, but there is none among men who has not sinned in thought, therefore the Psalmist says: "For the thought of man shall confess to thee"(b).

15.12.3.en: * "And hath put all things under his feet" (Eph 1:22)... Why all things? Why is it said that the angels, principalities, powers and all other powers, who never opposed the Lord, are put under His feet? The matter seems obscure. But the answer is that there is never anyone who is without sin. [The very stars are not clean in his sight] [15], and all creation trembles at the coming of the Lord... There is another explanation, which is that "all" does not refer to everyone but to those who are the subject of the dispute. Just as someone says: "All the citizens cried out," he does not mean by this that there was never anyone silent, but this is said of the majority that overwhelms the minority.

15.12.4.en: St. Jerome * [Behold, among his saints there is none unchangeable, and the heavens are not clean in his sight]. He repeats the name "the heavens," which is indicated by the title [saints]. It is written of these same saints: "The heavens declare the glory of God" (Ps 19:1). These are by nature subject to change. But when they earnestly desire to cleave always to the unchangeable Truth, by cleaving to Him they come to the crossing over (the heavenly life) to become unchangeable...

15.12.5.en: For what is this change but a kind of death? For it changes a thing into something else, and so it kills what it was in order to become what it was not. It is said of the Creator of all things: "Who only hath immortality" (1 Tim 6:16), as He alone is unchangeable in Himself. It is written of Him in James: "with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning" (Jas 1:17). For change itself is a shadow...

15.12.6.en: It was well said here: "the heavens are not clean in his sight," for in themselves, before the exact knowledge of God, even the preachers of purity cannot be perfect. As John testifies who says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8). If among the saints there is none who is unchangeable, and the heavens are not clean in His sight, who then claims for himself that he practices righteousness?

15.13.0.en: "How much more abominable and filthy is man, which drinketh iniquity like water!" [16]

15.13.1.en: If God does not entrust the saints with some of His works, such as salvation, how much more is the state of corrupt sinners who drink iniquity like water. Man finds his delight in iniquity as a thirsty man delights as he drinks water. And the wicked man reckons evil an integral part of his being, which he cannot do without, as a man needs water and cannot live without it.

15.13.2.en: * [How much more abominable and unprofitable is man, which drinketh iniquity like water!]... "Abominable" because of his uncleanness and stain, and "unprofitable" because of the evil of his imperfect life. "Abominable and unprofitable" can also be understood in another sense. Often the wicked man does something upright, but by practicing wrong things even the things he did uprightly become nothing...

15.13.3.en: What is eaten needs first to be chewed in order to be swallowed, but what is drunk has no obstacle before it... So the fool practices sin without drawing back, "drinking iniquity like water."

15.14.0.en: 17 "I will shew thee, hear me; and that which I have seen I will declare; 18 Which wise men have told from their fathers, and have not hid it: 19 Unto whom alone the earth was given, and no stranger passed among them. 20 The wicked man travaileth with pain all his days, and the number of years is hidden to the oppressor. 21 A dreadful sound is in his ears: in prosperity the destroyer shall come upon him. 22 He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness, and he is waited for of the sword. 23 He wandereth abroad for bread, saying, Where is it? he knoweth that the day of darkness is ready at his hand. 24 Trouble and anguish shall make him afraid; they shall prevail against him, as a king ready to the battle. 25 For he stretcheth out his hand against God, and strengtheneth himself against the Almighty. 26 He runneth upon him, even on his neck, upon the thick bosses of his bucklers: 27 Because he covereth his face with his fatness, and maketh collops of fat on his flanks. 28 And he dwelleth in desolate cities, and in houses which no man inhabiteth, which are ready to become heaps. 29 He shall not be rich, neither shall his substance continue, neither shall he prolong the perfection thereof upon the earth. 30 He shall not depart out of darkness; the flame shall dry up his branches, and by the breath of his mouth shall he go away. 31 Let not him that is deceived trust in vanity: for vanity shall be his recompence. 32 It shall be accomplished before his time, and his branch shall not be green. 33 He shall shake off his unripe grape as the vine, and shall cast off his flower as the olive. 34 For the congregation of hypocrites shall be desolate, and fire shall consume the tabernacles of bribery. 35 They conceive mischief, and bring forth vanity, and their belly prepareth deceit."

15.14.2.en: hear me; and that which I have seen I will declare" [17].

15.14.3.en: After belittling the person of Job, his conduct and his wisdom, he asked him to listen to him without protest on his part. He says to him: "I will shew thee," that is, I will explain to you what deserves to be heard, and I will present to you truths that I saw with my eyes and touched myself.

15.14.4.en: Since sin blinds the eyes of the wicked man, he thinks himself wise, and that there is none who can guide others like him. He is amazed how people do not profit from his wisdom, so he imposes himself on them as a teacher, and in conceit wants to teach all the time. Therefore James the Apostle says: "Be not many masters, my brethren" (Jas 3:1); rather it is fitting even for the teacher and all men of the priesthood to be lovers of continual learning.

15.14.5.en: [I will shew it to thee, hear me, and I will declare to thee what I have seen]. All the arrogant have this trait: when they have a sound concept, even a trifling one, they twist it to serve their pride. Instead of working to raise themselves on high in understanding, they fall into the pit of self-glorification, swallowed up by pride, and reckon themselves more learned than the learned. They seize for themselves esteem from those who approve of them, and use this to teach with authority those who are holier than they.

15.14.7.en: * In teaching others I desire to be able to learn, because there is one Master (God) who does not learn from what He teaches all. But men must learn before they teach, and receive from God their Teacher what they teach others.

15.14.8.en: As for me, I came from the judge's seat to the priesthood... and I had no opportunity to learn, therefore I had to learn and teach at the same time.

15.15.0.en: St. Ambrose "Which wise men have told from their fathers, and have not hid it." [18]

15.15.1.en: If the wise learn through the experience of their fathers without limiting themselves to their personal experiences, and so learn from the forebears through successive generations, and do not hide these experiences, then Eliphaz, who claims to be wise, presents these experiences to Job, even if they conflict with Job's experience or his personal understanding.

15.15.2.en: To what extent are we bound by what is found in the tradition of the Fathers?

15.15.3.en: The holy Fathers represent the mind of the catholic Church, which she received from the Apostles by the working of the Holy Spirit, who works without ceasing in the life of the Church. St. Augustine speaks of them, saying: [They held fast to what they found in the Church, they practiced what they had learned, and what they received from the Fathers they deposited in the hands of the children], [whoever despises the holy Fathers knows that he is despising the whole Church].

15.15.4.en: This authority rests on two factors: a natural factor, since the Fathers were characterized by a holy life and faithfulness in receiving the deposit of the living faith from the hands of the Apostles, therefore they are better able to bear witness to the life of the Church in all its aspects, especially since they hold one mind, in spite of the differences of cultures, gifts and circumstances, with the great distance between the apostolic sees and the difficulty of communications at that time. And the second factor is divine, for the Fathers lived led by the Holy Spirit, the Leader of the Church and her guide into all truth, who keeps her within the circle of the cross of Christ.

15.15.5.en: This does not mean the infallibility of the Fathers as individuals, but the catholic Church as a whole lives preserved by the Spirit of the Lord.

15.16.0.en: "Unto whom alone the earth was given, and no stranger passed among them." [19]

15.16.1.en: The wisdom that Eliphaz presents, which he received from his fathers, is the experience of trustworthy people in high positions, better able than others to manage the affairs of the earth, with whom no ignorant man, a stranger to the spirit of wisdom, shares. While Job said: "The earth is given into the hand of the wicked" (Job 9:24), Eliphaz says to him: [The earth is given into the hand of wise, holy, trustworthy men], and so it will remain in their hand, and not be given into the hand of a stranger to them. Here perhaps he hints that Job is neither wise nor holy nor a trustworthy person, otherwise the Sabeans and the Chaldeans, who are strangers, would not have plundered his wealth. And on the other hand, since Job lost his possessions, like one driven out of his distinguished position as a king or the chief of a tribe, he is not worthy to be among the wise to whom alone the earth was given.

15.16.2.en: Perhaps he refers here to the Church on earth, for those who manage her are the wise who walk in the spirit of the early Fathers, under the leadership of the Spirit of the holy God. And it is not fitting for there to be a stranger among them who does not have the true evangelical, ecclesial, spiritual spirit.

15.17.0.en: "The wicked man travaileth with pain all his days, and the number of years is hidden to the oppressor." [20]

15.17.1.en: Eliphaz almost says frankly and boldly that Job is a wicked man to whom the saying applies: "The wicked man travaileth with pain all his days, and the number of years is hidden to the oppressor." Thus he accuses Job of injustice and violence, so he has become worthy to writhe with harsh afflictions and trials; what he did has returned upon his head, so there is no longer time to pretend to be other than what he is within, for his days will not be long.

15.17.2.en: *Eliphaz the king of the Temanites, Bildad the tyrant of the Shuhites, and Zophar the king of the Minaeans (Mineans) rebuked Job violently on the ground that he suffered such punishments because of his sins. In their trivial outlook they did not perceive that the Lord had delivered him to be tried, so that he might be formed by the trials and receive a greater crown like a wrestler for Christ. Therefore they did not see this great mystery of wisdom. Their narrow hearts were afraid lest they should appear to be accusing God of injustice if they allowed that punishments could come upon a righteous man. They threw the responsibility on righteous Job for the punishments that had come upon him, saying: the whole life of the wicked passes in anxiety, and [the rich who gathers by injustice is vomited out] (Job 20:15). They claimed that he suffered all the sorrows, as a man suffering on earth because of his sins.

15.17.3.en: St. Ambrose * This saying is misleading, for we see many of the wicked living in prosperity and peace. Even if this does not last through all their lives, at least it occupies a large part of their lives (Jer 12:1). In any case Eliphaz wanted to correct the words of Job, who mocks the prosperity of the wicked. He also wanted at the same time to show that he himself was not wicked in living in prosperity.

15.17.4.en: [The years that are given to the oppressor are many]. In this too Eliphaz does not speak faithfully, for when God wills it He puts an end to the power of the oppressor; it is not bound by a number of years, nor limited by any time. He said this because Job said: [The just and blameless man is laughed to scorn, for at the appointed time he is made ready to die by the blows of the stranger, and sees his house destroyed by the wicked] (Job 12:4-5). Job wanted to speak of the time during which God allows sinners to torment the wicked (Wis 2:10) according to their ability (1 Cor 10:13), intending that each be tried according to his measure, declaring that they fight for virtue until they are crowned.

15.17.5.en: As for Eliphaz, he uttered these words against Job: [He gives many years to the strong], but this too is a misleading statement, like the following one. [And his terror is in his ears] (21): how can terror be in the ears of one who does not keep the law of God in his heart, and how does he not open his ears to those who could teach him the fear of God (Ps 37:31; 40:8; 34:12)?

15.17.6.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [And the number of the years of his injustice is uncertain]... It is known that every proud man practices tyranny according to his measure. What one practices in a state by virtue of his high position that suits him; another in a province, another in a city, another in his family, and another hides his evil and practices it on himself in the thought of his heart. For God is not concerned with the amount of evil that a man can practice, but the amount that is in his mind to practice. And when a man has no authority outwardly he is counted a tyrant inwardly, and iniquity rules him within. For although he does not oppress his relatives outwardly, inwardly he searches for an opportunity and authority to oppress others. For God looks at the hearts of men, so in God's eyes the wicked man is counted to have already practiced what he imagines.

15.17.8.en: "A dreadful sound is in his ears:

15.18.0.en: in prosperity (in an hour of peace) the destroyer shall come upon him." [21]

15.18.1.en: Eliphaz sees that Job should not be astonished that the sound of terrors does not leave his ears, for heaven and earth are requiting what he did before. He has no way to escape distress, for the sound of his evils pursues his ears, so he is like Cain, who believed that everyone who found him would slay him (Gen 4:14).

15.18.2.en: We do not deny that "there is no peace, saith the LORD, unto the wicked" (Isa 48:22). But the phrase here refers to the inner peace that sin takes away by isolating man from the source of his peace, while afflictions and troubles may intensify upon the saints to prove and sanctify them by the Spirit of the Lord, as they may intensify upon the wicked so that perhaps they may return to God by repentance.

15.18.3.en: As for outward peace and prosperity, we are not surprised if the Psalmist is astonished at the peace of the wicked, saying: "For I was envious of the proud, when I saw the peace of the wicked" (Ps 73:3). It is not true peace, for the writer of the Book of Wisdom says: "Moreover it was not enough for them that they erred in the knowledge of God; but they plunged into the great war of ignorance, and those so great evils they call peace" (Wis 14:22).

15.18.4.en: The Lord Christ came as Savior of the world, granting true inner peace to His believers.

15.18.5.en: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace" (Isa 9:6)

15.18.6.en: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!" (Isa 52:7)

15.18.7.en: "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed" (Isa 53:5)

15.18.8.en: "For the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but my kindness shall not depart from thee, neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed, saith the LORD that hath mercy on thee" (Isa 54:10)

15.18.9.en: "And I will make with them a covenant of peace, and will cause the evil beasts to cease out of the land: and they shall dwell safely in the wilderness, and sleep in the woods" (Ezek 34:25).

15.18.10.en: "Moreover I will make a covenant of peace with them; it shall be an everlasting covenant with them: and I will place them, and multiply them, and will set my sanctuary in the midst of them for evermore" (Ezek 37:26).

15.18.11.en: "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace! O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee; he is utterly cut off" (Nah 1:15).

15.18.12.en: "To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace" (Lk 1:79).

15.18.13.en: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men" (Lk 2:14).

15.18.14.en: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid" (Jn 14:27).

15.18.15.en: "These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world" (Jn 16:33).

15.18.16.en: * [A terrifying sound is always in his ears, and when there is peace he expects plots] [21]. But there is nothing happier than simplicity of heart... and nothing is terrifying in meeting with others. For simplicity is like a fortress of strength, and there is no doubt in passing through what has no remembrance of itself, therefore Solomon said well: "In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence," as he also says: [A secure mind is like a continual feast] (Prov 14:26; 15:15). For mere rest in safety is like a continual refreshment. On the other hand the evil mind is always in pains and toils, either because it struggles with trials that may come upon it, or fears that they may come upon it through others. Since it contrives plots against its relatives, the mind fears the plans that its relatives contrive against it... and when there is peace it dreads the occurrence of plots, since it always deals craftily, putting in its mind that no one deals simply with it. It is written: [When the wicked falls into the presence of the wicked he condemns] (Prov 18:3), for the darkness of his evil surrounds him, and consequently he despairs of there being light. Therefore it was said afterward: [He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness, but the sword awaits him] [22].
